claim: Asynchronous release persists for tens to hundreds of milliseconds after an action potential.
source: Asynchronous release is a ubiquitous form of neurotransmitter release that persists for tens to hundreds of milliseconds after an action potential.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a defining characteristic of asynchronous release.

claim: Approximately 75% of asynchronous events occurred inside the active zone.
source: ~75% of which occurred inside the AZ and with a bias towards the AZ center
evidence: This quantitative finding is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Approximately 25% of asynchronous events occurred outside of the functionally defined active zone (ectopically).
source: while ~25% occurred outside of the functionally defined AZ, that is, ectopically
evidence: This quantitative finding is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Ectopic asynchronous events occur at significantly longer time intervals from synchronous events than asynchronous events inside the AZ.
source: with ectopic events occurring at significantly longer time intervals from synchronous events than the asynchronous events inside the AZ
evidence: This temporal difference is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Both forms of asynchronous release did not, to a large extent, utilize the same release sites as synchronous events.
source: Both forms of asynchronous release did not, to a large extent, utilize the same release sites as synchronous events.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by clustering analysis in Figure 3.

claim: Asynchronous release has been ubiquitously observed in central synapses.
source: Asynchronous release has also been ubiquitously observed in central synapses and shown to regulate several major aspects of synaptic function, including spike timing precision, coincidence detection, and the duration of postsynaptic responses and excitability changes (Atluri and Regehr, 1998; Diamond and Jahr, 1995; Evstratova et al., 2014; Goda and Stevens, 1994; Hefft and Jonas, 2005; Lu and Trussell, 2000; Otsu and Murphy, 2004; Scheuss et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Asynchronous release regulates spike timing precision, coincidence detection, and the duration of postsynaptic responses and excitability changes.
source: Asynchronous release has also been ubiquitously observed in central synapses and shown to regulate several major aspects of synaptic function, including spike timing precision, coincidence detection, and the duration of postsynaptic responses and excitability changes (Atluri and Regehr, 1998; Diamond and Jahr, 1995; Evstratova et al., 2014; Goda and Stevens, 1994; Hefft and Jonas, 2005; Lu and Trussell, 2000; Otsu and Murphy, 2004; Scheuss et al., 2007).
evidence: This functional role is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The balance between synchronous and asynchronous release modulates signal processing in neural circuits.
source: the balance between the two components has been shown to modulate signal processing in neural circuits (Best and Regehr, 2009; Deng et al., 2020; Hefft and Jonas, 2005; Luo and Südhof, 2017; Medrihan et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Asynchronous events were observed to preferentially occur closer to the AZ center than synchronous release events in hippocampal boutons.
source: Asynchronous events were observed to preferentially occur closer to the AZ center than synchronous release events (Kusick et al., 2020)
evidence: This is a finding from a previous flash-and-freeze EM study cited in the introduction.

claim: Asynchronous release events have a preferential transsynaptic alignment with postsynaptic NMDA receptors that are clustered near the center of the postsynaptic density.
source: and to have a preferential transsynaptic alignment with postsynaptic NMDA receptors that are clustered near the center of the postsynaptic density (Li et al., 2021)
evidence: This is a finding from a previous flash-and-freeze EM study cited in the introduction.

claim: A live imaging study using SF-iGluSnFR showed that asynchronous release events are more broadly distributed across the presynaptic area than synchronous release.
source: This study reached an opposite conclusion, showing that asynchronous release events are more broadly distributed across the presynaptic area than synchronous release, localize further away from the AZ center, and cover a larger area of the AZ (Mendonça et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous live imaging study cited in the introduction.

claim: Individual release events were localized with ~27 nm localization precision.
source: Individual AP-evoked release events were robustly detected and localized with ~27 nm localization precision throughout the observation time period (Figure 1Aii) as we described previously (Maschi et al., 2018; Maschi and Klyachko, 2017).
evidence: This technical specification is stated in the Results section and references previous methodological papers.

claim: 98% of synapses had asynchronous events inside the AZ.
source: The vast majority (98%) of synapses had asynchronous events inside the AZ
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the Results section.

claim: 79% of synapses displayed ectopic asynchronous events during the observation period.
source: and 79% of synapses displayed ectopic asynchronous events during our observation period (Figure 1E)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Approximately 73% of asynchronous events were localized inside the AZ, and approximately 27% were localized ectopically.
source: When comparing among asynchronous events, ~73% were localized 'in-AZ,' and ~27% were localized ectopically (Figure 1F).
evidence: This quantitative finding is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The spatial distribution of asynchronous events cannot simply arise randomly.
source: This spatial distribution of asynchronous events cannot simply arise randomly since modeled events distributed randomly in the same boutons (see 'Materials and methods') follow a significantly different distribution (p<0.0001, two-sample K-S test; Figure 1F, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison with simulated random distributions, shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The subgroup of asynchronous events inside the AZ was localized significantly closer to the AZ center than the synchronous events in the same synapses.
source: Moreover, in contrast to the entire population of asynchronous events, a subgroup of these events inside the AZ was localized significantly closer to the AZ center than the synchronous events in the same synapses (p<0.0001, two-sample K-S test; Figure 1G vs. C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The error of event localization was nearly the same for synchronous and asynchronous release events either inside or outside of the AZ.
source: Moreover, the error of event localization (i.e. spatial precision of localization) was nearly the same for synchronous and asynchronous release events either inside or outside of the AZ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The functional definition of the AZ limits is in close agreement with the ultrastructural measurements of the AZ dimensions in hippocampal synapses.
source: Our current definition is in close agreement with the ultrastructural measurements of the AZ dimensions in these synapses (Maschi and Klyachko, 2017; Schikorski and Stevens, 1997)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The proportion of asynchronous events inside the AZ reached an asymptote of ~83%.
source: In contrast, we found that this proportion reached an asymptote of ~83% (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), indicating that ~17% of asynchronous release still occurs outside of the functionally defined AZ limits.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Near-TIRF imaging with 25 ms/frame acquisition showed essentially the same results as 50 ms/frame recordings, including the presence of ~35% of ectopic release among asynchronous events.
source: We observed essentially the same results as above, including the presence of ~35% of ectopic release among asynchronous events (Figure 1H)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The properties of asynchronous release were very similar for three temporal windows examined (25-50 ms, 50-75 ms, and 75-100 ms).
source: We also found that the properties of asynchronous release were very similar for the three temporal windows examined, with a slight increase in the proportion of ectopic vs. 'in-AZ' asynchronous events with time, from 33% to 37% to 39% for the three time windows, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of data in Figure 1H and 1I.

claim: Ectopic events are more likely to occur with longer time delays.
source: This result suggests that ectopic events are more likely to occur with longer time delays (explored in more details below).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and further explored in Figure 4.

claim: Using SF-iGluSnFR(A184S), approximately 71% of asynchronous events were localized inside the AZ, while approximately 29% were localized ectopically.
source: In close agreement with the above results, we observed two populations of asynchronous events: ~71% of which were localized inside the AZ, while ~29% were localized ectopically (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: The subpopulation of asynchronous events inside the AZ had a strong spatial bias toward the AZ center when measured with SF-iGluSnFR.
source: Moreover, the subpopulation of asynchronous events inside the AZ had a strong spatial bias toward the AZ center (Figure 2D), further supporting the above results.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Measurements with SF-iGluSnFR have an intrinsically lower localization precision (by approximately threefold) compared to vGlut1-pHluorin.
source: Thus measurements with SF-iGluSnFR have an intrinsically lower localization precision (by approximately threefold) comparing to vGlut1-pHluorin.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a technical limitation.

claim: Hierarchical clustering revealed 8.9 ± 0.2 clusters/release sites per AZ.
source: Clustering of synchronous events using a hierarchical clustering algorithm with 50 nm diameter (see 'Materials and methods') revealed 8.9 ± 0.2 clusters/release sites per AZ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There were 2.8 ± 0.1 repeatedly reused release sites per AZ (with two or more events detected).
source: or 2.8 ± 0.1 repeatedly reused release sites per AZ (with two or more events detected) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: For the subpopulation of asynchronous events localized inside the AZ, only 25.4% occurred at release sites defined by synchronous events.
source: This analysis showed that, for the subpopulation of asynchronous events localized inside the AZ, only 25.4% occurred at release sites defined by synchronous events (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The overall overlap of synchronous and asynchronous release in the same release sites is only ~15%.
source: Considering that ~27% of asynchronous release events are ectopic and by definition do not utilize the release sites involved in synchronous release, the overall overlap of two forms of release in the same release sites is only ~15%.
evidence: This is calculated from the data and stated in the Results section.

claim: Using nearest-neighbor analysis, only ~20% of asynchronous events were localized within 50 nm from a synchronous event.
source: Similar to the clustering analysis above, we observed that only ~20% of asynchronous events were localized within 50 nm from a synchronous event (Figure 3D)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Ectopic asynchronous events display significantly longer time intervals from either the preceding synchronous events or the subsequent synchronous events compared to asynchronous events within the AZ.
source: We found that the ectopic asynchronous events display significantly longer time intervals from either the preceding synchronous events (Figure 4A) or the subsequent synchronous events (Figure 4B) compared to asynchronous events within the AZ.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: There were no temporal differences for asynchronous events detected inside and outside of release sites when only the subpopulation of asynchronous events inside the AZ was considered.
source: When only the subpopulation of asynchronous events inside the AZ was considered, we did not observe temporal differences for events detected inside and outside of release sites (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: The fluorescence decay of the average release events had two clearly distinct kinetic components (~60 ms and ~800 ms).
source: The fluorescence decay of the average release events had two clearly distinct kinetic components (~60 ms and ~800 ms) (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The two kinetic components of fluorescence decay (~60 ms and ~800 ms) are in close agreement with previous studies identifying these as ultrafast and fast endocytosis.
source: in close agreement with previous studies identifying these two components as ultrafast and fast endocytosis, respectively (Balaji and Ryan, 2007; Chanaday and Kavalali, 2018; Leitz and Kavalali, 2011; Leitz and Kavalali, 2014)
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: For synchronous events, ultrafast and fast components represented ~58% and ~42% of signal decay, respectively.
source: For synchronous events, ultrafast and fast components represented ~58% and ~42% of signal decay, respectively
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The average synchronous event amplitude was significantly larger than asynchronous event amplitude (p<0.001).
source: Further quantification of the average synchronous vs asynchronous event traces revealed significantly larger average synchronous event amplitude (p<0.001, Figure 5—figure supplement 1H)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The fast component of decay was significantly larger for synchronous than for asynchronous events.
source: and major differences in the fast component of decay, which was significantly larger for synchronous than for asynchronous events (Figure 5C and D)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: There were no significant differences in ultrafast component of endocytosis between synchronous and asynchronous events.
source: In contrast, we found no significant differences in ultrafast component of endocytosis between the two types of release (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: There were no differences observed in endocytosis kinetics between the two subpopulations of asynchronous events, 'in-AZ' vs. ectopic.
source: There were also no differences observed in endocytosis kinetics between the two subpopulations of asynchronous events, 'in-AZ' vs. ectopic (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: There was a significant increase in the amplitude of synchronous events with distance from the center of the AZ toward periphery.
source: Surprisingly, we observed a significant increase in the amplitude of synchronous events with distance from the center of the AZ toward periphery (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Asynchronous events did not show any measurable differences in amplitude across the AZ.
source: In contrast, asynchronous events in the same synapses did not show any measurable differences in amplitude across the AZ (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The distance-dependent increase in synchronous event amplitude was largely abolished by pre-incubation with 100 µM EGTA-AM.
source: Importantly, the distance-dependent increase in synchronous event amplitude was largely abolished by pre-incubation with 100 µM EGTA-AM (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: There was a strong (0.98) and highly significant (p=0.015) correlation between synchronous event amplitude and distance to the AZ center.
source: We observed a strong (0.98) and highly significant (p=0.015) correlation for synchronous release
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on Pearson's linear correlation analysis.

claim: There was no significant correlation found between asynchronous event amplitude and distance to the AZ center (p=0.92).
source: while there was no significant correlation found for asynchronous release (p=0.92; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on Pearson's linear correlation analysis.

claim: Application of dyngo-4a eliminated the differences in average event amplitude between synchronous and asynchronous release.
source: Nevertheless, we observed that dyngo-4a eliminated the differences in average event amplitude between synchronous and asynchronous release (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: For synchronous events, there was an increase in the fast component of decay with the distance from the AZ center.
source: For synchronous events, we found an increase in the fast component of decay with the distance from the AZ center (Figure 5H, bottom)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The ultrafast component of decay remained unaltered across the AZ for synchronous events.
source: while the ultrafast component of decay remained unaltered across the AZ (Figure 5H, top)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The distance dependence of the fast component of decay for synchronous events was eliminated by pre-incubation with EGTA-AM.
source: Notably, this distance dependence of the fast component of decay was eliminated by pre-incubation with EGTA-AM (Figure 5I)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5I.

claim: For asynchronous release events, both ultrafast and fast components of decay were homogeneous across the AZ and did not correlate with the distance to AZ center.
source: In contrast, for asynchronous release events, both ultrafast and fast components of decay were homogeneous across the AZ and did not correlate with the distance to AZ center (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Both ultrafast and fast components of decay were no longer different between synchronous and asynchronous events in the presence of EGTA-AM.
source: Moreover, as was the case with the event amplitude, both ultrafast and fast components of decay were no longer different between synchronous and asynchronous events in the presence of EGTA-AM (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5I.

claim: In the absence of MVR events, there was still a distance-dependent increase in the event amplitude and in the fast component of endocytosis for synchronous but not asynchronous release events.
source: In contrast with the above prediction, in the absence of MVR events, we still observed a distance-dependent increase in the event amplitude, and in the fast component of endocytosis, and this was the case for synchronous but not asynchronous release events (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: For synchronous events, 65% of boutons showed a positive correlation between event amplitude and distance to the AZ center.
source: We observed that for synchronous events 65% of boutons showed a positive correlation
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5J.

claim: For synchronous events, the proportion of boutons with positive correlation increased to 68% when only UVR events were included in the analysis.
source: which was further increased to 68% when only UVR events were included in the analysis (Figure 5J)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5J.

claim: The presence of EGTA-AM effectively eliminated the positive correlation between synchronous event amplitude and distance to the AZ center, bringing down the number of boutons with a positive correlation to chance (48%).
source: In line with the population analyses above, the presence of EGTA-AM effectively eliminated this phenomenon, bringing down the number of boutons with a positive correlation to chance (48%) (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5J.

claim: For asynchronous events, the number of boutons with a positive correlation between event amplitude and distance to the AZ center was no higher than chance (52%).
source: Also, similarly to the population analysis, for asynchronous events, the number of boutons with a positive correlation was no higher than chance (52%) (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5J.

claim: The average spatial profile of synchronous release events had a similar width near the AZ center vs. periphery.
source: The average spatial profile of synchronous release events had a similar width near the AZ center vs. periphery (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The membrane diffusion coefficient decreases approximately tenfold with the decrease in temperature from 37°C to room temperature.
source: In addition, we considered that the membrane diffusion coefficient decreases approximately tenfold with the decrease in temperature from 37°C to room temperature (Ries et al., 2009)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The event spatial profile was nearly the same at 37°C and room temperature over the first three frames (150 ms).
source: In contrast, we found that the event spatial profile was nearly the same at the two temperatures over the first three frames (150 ms) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C–F)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C-F.

claim: Photobleaching accounted only for ~3.3% of event decay during 1 s interval.
source: Finally, photobleaching accounted only for ~3.3% of event decay during 1 s interval
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Sr2+ enhances asynchronous release approximately three- to fourfold due to its slower clearance rate and differential affinity to Syt1 in comparison to calcium.
source: Sr2+ enhances asynchronous release approximately three- to fourfold due to its slower clearance rate and differential affinity to Syt1 in comparison to calcium (Atluri and Regehr, 1998; Goda and Stevens, 1994; Rumpel and Behrends, 1999; Xu-Friedman and Regehr, 1999; Dürst et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Sr2+ application caused a significant reduction in synchronous release (p=0.0042).
source: Indeed, we found that Sr2+ application caused a significant reduction in synchronous release (p=0.0042, two-sample K-S test)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Sr2+ application caused an increase in asynchronous release inside the AZ (p=0.028).
source: and an increase in asynchronous release inside the AZ (p=0.028, two-sample K-S test; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: In the presence of Sr2+, 76.5% of asynchronous events were located inside the AZ and 23.5% occurred ectopically.
source: In the presence of Sr2+, 76.5% of asynchronous events were located inside the AZ and 23.5% occurred ectopically
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The spatial distribution of asynchronous events in Sr2+ conditions was not statistically different from control conditions (p=0.79).
source: In fact, we did not find statistical differences between the spatial distributions of asynchronous events in the two conditions, neither for normalized distances (Figure 6A) nor for the absolute distances (Figure 6C) (p=0.79, K-S test).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: In the presence of Sr2+, the subpopulation of asynchronous events inside the AZ was localized significantly closer to the AZ center than synchronous events in the same synapses (p=0.0067).
source: Also, similarly to our earlier observations, in the presence of Sr2+ the subpopulation of asynchronous events inside the AZ was localized significantly closer to the AZ center than synchronous events in the same synapses (p=0.0067, K-S test; Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The proportion of asynchronous events inside the AZ that utilize the same release sites as synchronous events increased from ~25% to 31% in Sr2+ conditions.
source: The proportion of asynchronous events inside the AZ that utilize the same release sites as synchronous events was also similar to what we observed above in control conditions, with a modest increment (from ~25% to 31%, Figure 6D)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In the presence of Sr2+, the average fluorescence traces for synchronous and asynchronous events were indistinguishable from each other.
source: In contrast with the large differences in the decay kinetics between the two forms of release in control (normal) conditions, the average fluorescence traces for synchronous and asynchronous events were indistinguishable from each other in the presence of Sr2+ (Figure 6E)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: In the presence of Sr2+, the endocytosis kinetics of synchronous events became indistinguishable from asynchronous events in normal conditions.
source: In fact, in the presence of Sr2+, the endocytosis kinetics of synchronous events became indistinguishable from asynchronous events in normal conditions (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The distance-dependent increase in synchronous event amplitude and in the contribution of fast endocytosis was no longer observed in Sr2+.
source: Moreover, the distance-dependent increase in synchronous event amplitude and in the contribution of fast endocytosis was no longer observed in Sr2+ (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6H.

claim: The average traces of asynchronous events were similar in the presence of Sr2+ to those in control conditions.
source: In contrast, the average traces of asynchronous events were similar in the presence of Sr2+ to those in control conditions (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6F.

claim: No distance dependence of decay kinetics was observed for asynchronous events in the presence of Sr2+.
source: Also, similarly to control conditions, no distance dependence of decay kinetics was observed for asynchronous events in the presence of Sr2+ (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Ectopic synchronous release has been observed in several types of synapses, including cerebellar synapses, ribbon-type synapses, and several glutamatergic and cholinergic sensory synapses.
source: Although, to the best of our knowledge, ectopic asynchronous release has not been previously reported, there is extensive evidence for ectopic synchronous release occurring outside of the ultrastructurally defined AZ in several types of synapses, including cerebellar synapses (Matsui and Jahr, 2003; Matsui and Jahr, 2004; Matsui et al., 2005), ribbon-type synapses (Lenzi et al., 2002; Zenisek et al., 2000), and several glutamatergic and cholinergic sensory synapses (Balakrishnan et al., 2014; Balakrishnan et al., 2011; Coggan et al., 2005; Fu and Sretavan, 2012; Thyssen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Synchronous ectopic release was found to rely on a different proportion of voltage-gated Ca2+ channel (VGCC) subtypes than release within the AZ.
source: Synchronous ectopic release was found to rely on a different proportions of voltage-gated Ca2+ channel (VGCC) subtypes than release within the AZ (Matsui and Jahr, 2004)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: Ectopic synchronous release exhibits different release probability and short-term plasticity compared to release within the AZ.
source: and to exhibit different release probability and short-term plasticity (Dobson and Bellamy, 2015)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: Release sites are associated with nanoclusters of SNARE proteins and docking machinery.
source: Indeed, at the level of molecular organization, release sites are associated with the nanoclusters of SNARE proteins and docking machinery (Gramlich and Klyachko, 2019)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: SNARE protein nanoclusters are not limited to the AZ, but are also commonly present at extrasynaptic locations including the axons.
source: and extensive evidence indicates that these nanoclusters are not limited to the AZ, but are also commonly present at extrasynaptic locations including the axons (Garcia et al., 1995; Sesack and Snyder, 1995; Hagiwara et al., 2005)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by multiple citations.

claim: STED measurements showed that clusters of Syntaxin-1A are found all over the synaptic membrane at the neuromuscular junctions, well beyond the boundaries of the AZ.
source: Moreover, STED measurements showed that clusters of a SNARE protein Syntaxin-1A are found all over the synaptic membrane at the neuromuscular junctions, well beyond the boundaries of the AZ (Ribrault et al., 2011; Ullrich et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Syntaxin-1A clusters are more abundant, stable, and larger in size inside the AZ in comparison to ectopic clusters.
source: Syntaxin-1A clusters are more abundant, stable, and larger in size inside the AZ in comparison to ectopic clusters (Ullrich et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: Syntaxin-1A co-clusters with the L-type VGCCs.
source: Syntaxin-1A co-clusters with the L-type VGCCs (Sajman et al., 2017)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: The smaller outside clusters of Syntaxin-1A may serve as sites of ectopic release.
source: suggesting that the smaller outside clusters may serve as sites of ectopic release (Ullrich et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculation supported by a citation.

claim: Flash-freeze EM studies suggested entirely distinct organization of synchronous and asynchronous release with a preferential trans-synaptic alignment of asynchronous release events with a cluster of NMDA receptors near the AZ center, while synchronous events align with more peripherally located clusters of AMPA receptors.
source: Flash-freeze EM studies suggested entirely distinct organization of the two forms of release with a preferential trans-synaptic alignment of asynchronous release events with a cluster of NMDA receptors near the AZ center, while synchronous events align with more peripherally located clusters of AMPA receptors (Kusick et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Live imaging studies with SF-iGluSnFR observed ~50% overlap of synchronous and asynchronous release at the same release sites.
source: In contrast, live imaging studies with SF-iGluSnFR observed ~50% overlap of the two forms of release at the same release sites, pointing to a large degree of overlap, and arguing against preferential alignment with two spatially segregated types of receptors (Mendonça et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: The two forms of release can overlap at the same release sites, but only in ~15–20% of the cases, at least within the limited observation time window.
source: Our results again are compatible with and largely reconcile the two previous studies by showing that the two forms of release can overlap at the same release sites, but only in ~15–20% of the cases, at least within our limited observation time window.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a synthesis of the current findings.

claim: Analyses of release site utilization must be limited to ~120–150 s by the random natural displacement of synapses in culture, which has a rate of ~20–25 nm/min.
source: We previously found that analyses of release site utilization in our culture conditions, which are similar to the above study (Mendonça et al., 2022), must be limited to ~120–150 s by the random natural displacement of synapses in culture, which has a rate of ~20–25 nm/min (Maschi and Klyachko, 2017)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Longer recordings cause a progressively increasing blur in the definition of release sites based on event clustering, effectively broadening the release site dimensions and thus overestimating the spatial overlap between the two forms of release.
source: As a result, longer recordings cause a progressively increasing blur in the definition of release sites based on event clustering, effectively broadening the release site dimensions and thus overestimating the spatial overlap between the two forms of release.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference about methodological limitations.

claim: The cluster diameter used in the current study is derived independently from biological considerations by calculating the inconsistency coefficient, giving the value for the natural cluster diameter of ~50 nm.
source: The cluster diameter used in our studies is derived independently from any biological considerations by calculating the inconsistency coefficient, as required by the algorithm (Wang et al., 2016), giving the value for the natural cluster diameter in our data of ~50 nm (Maschi and Klyachko, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: The localization precision reported for SF-iGluSnFR of ~75 nm does not permit event clustering with effective diameter smaller than 150 nm.
source: The localization precision reported for SF-iGluSnFR of ~75 nm (Mendonça et al., 2022) does not permit event clustering with effective diameter smaller than 150 nm.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference about methodological limitations.

claim: Given the average AZ dimensions of only ~250 nm, the cluster diameter of 150 nm would encompass a large proportion of the AZ, thus likely overestimating the degree of overlap between the two forms of release.
source: Given the average AZ dimensions of only ~250 nm (Ackermann et al., 2015), the cluster diameter of 150 nm would encompass a large proportion of the AZ, thus likely overestimating the degree of overlap between the two forms of release.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference about methodological limitations.

claim: Synchronous and asynchronous events can indeed overlap at the same release sites, but to a large extent are spatially segregated.
